purpose: Score CloakBrowser at ITS ACTUAL JOB: pages that REFUSE a plain client.
why_this_corpus_exists: The 26-query free-tier run (eval/results/20260803T134932Z.md) recorded its own
biggest gap in plain words: 'ddgs did not block once across either run, so
there was nothing to bypass. On this corpus CloakBrowser is scored purely as
an extractor; its stealth value is UNMEASURED, not disproven.'
That corpus asked general-knowledge questions and landed on Wikipedia, which
no one bot-walls. This one is built the opposite way: every URL is chosen
BECAUSE it is expected to resist a plain fetch. If CloakBrowser cannot beat
these, the fallback tier does not earn its ~553 MB.
URLS ARE DISCOVERED, NOT INVENTED. Every one came out of a live ddgs search
on 2026-08-03 (see run_botwall.py --discovery). A hand-guessed product URL
that 404s would be scored as a wall, which would be a fabricated finding.
expectation_is_a_hypothesis_not_a_label: `expect` records what we PREDICT before running, so the table can show where
the prediction was wrong. A corpus that only ever confirms itself measures
nothing. Several of these are expected to be READABLE by plain httpx —
they are the controls. A run where every single URL is walled cannot tell a
working bot-wall detector from one that returns True.

urls.note: BWS product page for the Emu Export 375mL can. Endeavour runs Akamai + a store-scoped price, so the number is geo/store dependent even when the page reads.
Same SKU, same corporate stack as BWS. Included as the PAIR CONTROL: two sites behind one bot-wall vendor should behave alike, and if they do not, the finding is about the page, not the wall.
Liquorland product page, 30-can block. Coles Group front end.
First Choice carries the same Coles SKU id (6517858) on the same URL shape. If this 404s, that is itself the finding — the two banners do not actually share a catalogue path.
Coles supermarket listing of the same block. Historically one of the hardest Australian walls (Imperva/Incapsula).
Independent-banner group. Lighter stack than the majors — a genuine test of whether the corpus can distinguish 'walled' from 'merely dynamic'.

Bottlemart has no per-product URL in search results — its specials live in a store-scoped catalogue behind a locator. The landing page is the honest entry point, and 'you cannot get a price without picking a store' is a real result.

A DIRECT Geraldton competitor with a real per-product page. Small independent site — expected READABLE, and included as the positive control: if the chain reports this as walled, the wall detector is broken.
Another direct Geraldton competitor. Store-scoped SPA storefront. Its front page carries a live beer-specials block that DOES list the Emu Export 30-block, so it is a price test after all.
KNOWN REGRESSION. The 2026-08-03 run recorded 'Page.content failed because the SPA was still navigating (fixable with a settle wait)'. This URL exists to prove or disprove that fix.
KNOWN REGRESSION. The same run recorded 'thespruceeats.com returned no text at all'. Second settle-wait test case.
WA news front page — client-rendered, metered paywall, heavy consent gating. The news-SPA slot.

target_note: `target` is the string that must appear — WITH a price within 600 characters
of it — for a read to count as having got THE page rather than A page.
This column was added mid-run because the generic meaningful-content
heuristic was measured OVERSTATING: Jina's read of the BWS product page
scored 20,000 chars and 278 price tokens while containing neither the
product nor its price. The entire extract was navigation chrome and filter
facets ($10/$20/$50... are price-range filters). Length is not evidence.
`null` means the entry is a rendering test rather than a price test — the
question there is whether a browser can see the page at all.
